entry_point.core_concept: mechanical equilibrium as potential energy minimization
entry_point.discipline_context: static mechanical systems relax toward equilibrium by reducing potential energy, so gradient descent is taught as a numerical relaxation method for energy surfaces.
entry_point.rationale: Second-year mechanical engineering students know potential energy, equilibrium and basic Python, so the lesson should begin in the language of energy, forces and stability before introducing formal optimization vocabulary.

chapter_sequence.title: Potential Energy, Equilibrium, and the Optimization Problem
chapter_sequence.purpose: Introduce the mechanical interpretation of minimization, stationary points, and equilibrium using potential energy and force balance.

chapter_sequence.title: Gradient Descent as Numerical Relaxation
chapter_sequence.purpose: Present the iterative update rule as a relaxation method and connect gradients to mechanical forces.

chapter_sequence.title: Step Size, Stability, and Energy Decrease
chapter_sequence.purpose: Explain step-size choices, the descent lemma, and energy decrease in terms of mechanical stability.
source_locators: Section 3.3 Convergence Analysis for L-Smooth Convex Functions

chapter_sequence.title: Bowl-Shaped Energy Surfaces and Strong Stability
chapter_sequence.purpose: Use convexity and strong convexity to describe well-behaved energy wells and linear convergence in engineering terms.
source_locators: Section 3.4 Convergence Analysis for μ-Strongly Convex Functions

chapter_sequence.title: Momentum, Acceleration, and Practical Relaxation
chapter_sequence.purpose: Introduce momentum-based updates as damped dynamic relaxation and show how acceleration can improve convergence for stiff systems.

chapter_sequence.title: Advanced Relaxation Tools and Implementation Notes
chapter_sequence.purpose: Summarize adaptive and second-order methods as advanced tools and link them to code and practical numerical simulation.

discipline_bridges.domain_mapping: map the gradient of potential energy to the mechanical force vector acting on a configuration.
discipline_bridges.analogy_boundary: This bridge holds when the system is conservative and described by a scalar potential; it does not apply to non-conservative forces or dynamics with friction that are not derived from a potential.

discipline_bridges.domain_mapping: map a minimizer to a stable equilibrium of a mechanical system where potential energy is lowest.
discipline_bridges.analogy_boundary: The analogy is exact only for static equilibrium in conservative systems; it does not cover saddle points or unstable equilibrium.

discipline_bridges.domain_mapping: map the step size to a relaxation parameter or damping/time-step size used when moving a system toward equilibrium.
discipline_bridges.analogy_boundary: A too-large step size can cause overshoot like a too-large time step in explicit dynamics, but the numerical method is not literally time integration unless specifically interpreted as one.

implementation_strategy: Use simple Python code and NumPy arrays to compute gradients and update coordinates.
Tie each algorithm update rule to an explicit code block so students can see the correspondence.
Use a quadratic energy example that is easy to evaluate and plot to demonstrate convergence.
Explain the meaning of variables and operations in mechanical terms.
assessment_strategy: ask learners to relate gradient descent updates to force balance in a spring system.
include a computational exercise with a quadratic potential and fixed step size.
ask learners to compare constant step size with momentum-based relaxation.
include an advanced conceptual exercise on the role of strong convexity and condition number.

coverage_decisions.reason: This section provides the core minimization problem and stationary condition needed for the mechanical equilibrium framing.
Smoothness is introduced after the physical energy framing to explain energy decrease and step-size stability.
Convexity and strong convexity are used to describe stable energy wells and convergence properties.
The update rule is central to the numerical relaxation interpretation.
Step-size choices are essential to make the method practical and stable.

coverage_decisions.source_locator: Section 3.3 Convergence Analysis for L-Smooth Convex Functions
coverage_decisions.reason: The O(1/k) energy decrease result supports the mechanical relaxation explanation.

coverage_decisions.source_locator: Section 3.4 Convergence Analysis for μ-Strongly Convex Functions
coverage_decisions.reason: Strong convexity is linked to linear convergence in a stiff engineering system.
Momentum is valuable as a practical relaxation extension for stiff systems.
Nesterov acceleration is included as an advanced acceleration technique.
Stochastic and adaptive methods are preserved at a high level while keeping the main lesson focused on deterministic relaxation.
Newton and quasi-Newton methods provide useful context for more advanced energy minimization approaches.
Exercises support student practice and connect to the adapted mechanical examples.
